summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is a web tool that tells anyone whether a place on Earth is really changing, and how sure we can be. Users click one of seven regions on an interactive map, such as the Sahel, the Aral Sea or the Arctic; they choose NASA variables like temperature, rainfall, soil moisture or aerosols; and they get monthly time series and a plain-language verdict: the rate of change per decade, a confidence range and statistical significance. 

Seasons are removed and autocorrelation is corrected for, so noise is not mistaken for a trend. Regions and variables can be compared side by side, and guided demos show how a conclusion can change. It addresses the challenge by turning decades of NASA MERRA-2, GPM IMERG and GLDAS data into understandable evidence, helping students, planners and the public separate real environmental change from natural variability.
details:
What it does and how it works

You start on a world map where seven regions are highlighted with soft coloured shapes that follow their real outlines. Hovering shows what the region is and which variables are available. Clicking opens it. You pick variables, and the app shows each one as a monthly series with the seasonal cycle removed, a 12-month average and a fitted trend line.

Behind the chart is a statistics engine. It subtracts each calendar month’s long-term average to remove seasons, then runs a linear fit, a Mann-Kendall trend test and Sen’s slope. All of them are adjusted for month-to-month autocorrelation, which otherwise makes trends look more certain than they are. The result is a headline verdict such as “a significant increasing trend of 0.3 °C per decade”, with a confidence range, a p-value and a small interval “ruler” showing the range against zero. I tested the method by simulation: on data with no trend and realistic autocorrelation it raises false alarms about 4 to 5% of the time, as it should at a 5% level.

Users can change the years analysed and the confidence level (90, 95 or 99%) and watch the verdict change. They can also compare several variables in one region, or one variable across regions, with a flag when two regions have significant trends in opposite directions. Five guided demos walk through real examples. Their text never states a result: every number is filled in from live data, so the demos cannot go out of date.

The data are cached ahead of time. A script downloads NASA’s monthly files, averages each region, and saves small tables. The live app serves only those tables, so it is fast and does not depend on NASA’s servers being available.

Benefits and intended impact

  • It lowers the barrier to Earth-science data. A student or local planner can ask “is my region getting drier?” without writing code or knowing statistics.
  • Variable explainers and the start-year demos show how trends can be misread.
  • Every verdict shows its margin of error, and the app states plainly when the evidence is weak, when a window is too short, and when data are synthetic.
  • It is open source, so teachers or researchers can add regions and variables by editing two small catalogue files.

The intended impact is more people reading environmental change from evidence rather than anecdote, and a reusable base for a fuller NASA data explorer.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: Python and JavaScript.
  • Backend: pandas, NumPy, SciPy and pymannkendall for the analysis. FastAPI is the reference API and Flask serves it in production, with the same endpoints and JSON verified by tests. earthaccess and xarray download and read NASA files.
  • Frontend: React and Vite, MapLibre GL for the map, Plotly for charts. The region washes are drawn in code: each real outline is rasterised, and a distance transform fades its opacity from a faint edge to a stronger core.
  • Hosting: PythonAnywhere for the backend, Netlify for the frontend, and GitHub for the code.
  • Testing: 33 backend tests, frontend unit tests, and Monte Carlo simulation of the statistics.
  • AI assistance: I used Claude as a coding and writing assistant, and tested the results ourselves.

Creative aspects of the app?

  • The map shows real region shapes with soft gradients that melt into the basemap, instead of rectangles or pins.
  • The verdict is the first thing you see, with the evidence beneath it. Technical statistics are available but not required to understand the result.
  • The demos are generated from live results, and several are built to show a limitation, such as a trend that depends on the start year.
  • It is built to be honest: a banner flags synthetic data, and the app says which rectangle the numbers are averaged over.

Factors I considered

  • Statistical validity: autocorrelation, seasonality and short records. I checked the method by simulation rather than trusting a textbook formula.
  • Reliability for the demo: cached data and a small footprint, so the app works without live NASA access.
  • Honesty about limits: the statistics use rectangles that enclose each region rather than the exact outline, some outlines (such as the Amazon arc) are approximations, and MERRA-2 and GLDAS are models constrained by observations, not raw measurements. These limits are stated in the app and the README on Github.
  • Cost and access: only free services are used, and the Earthdata account is needed only to rebuild the data.

Source code: https://github.com/m-j-r-q/Earth-System-Trend-Detective

Live App: https://earthsystemtrenddetective.netlify.app/
